title: Asking rents range from about $1,040 to $2,280 for a 1-bedroom, and advertised rents are usually above what the CMHC survey finds tenants pay
question: Where are rents lower, how have they changed, and how do advertised rents compare with what existing tenants pay?
dek: What a new lease costs on listing sites in 2026-Q2, how it moved in the past year and since 2019, and how it compares with CMHC's survey of rents actually charged.

findings.headline: 1-bedroom asking rents run from $1,040 in Sherbrooke to $2,280 in Vancouver
findings.detail: Average advertised rent for a 1-bedroom apartment in 2026-Q2 across the 26 of our 31 places that the table covers: median $1,500; the five lowest are Sherbrooke ($1,040), Québec City ($1,210), Saint John ($1,230), Regina ($1,250), Edmonton ($1,260); the five highest are Vancouver ($2,280), Toronto ($2,090), Victoria ($2,040), Ottawa ($1,900), Kelowna ($1,880). Asking rent applies to units currently advertised, so it is the price a new arrival would see on listing sites, not what long-term tenants pay. Charlottetown, Brandon, Whitehorse, Yellowknife and Iqaluit are not in this table (CMAs only).
findings.calc: Table 46-10-0092-01, 'Apartment - 1 bedroom', 'Average asking rent', REF_DATE 2026-04 (2026-Q2); sorted ascending over places with a published value; median over 26 places.

findings.headline: Over the past year 1-bedroom asking rents fell in 14 of 24 places, led by Calgary, Abbotsford–Mission, Kitchener–Waterloo
findings.detail: Change in the 1-bedroom average asking rent, 2026-Q2 vs 2025-Q2: median -2.1%. Largest falls: Calgary -6.1%, Abbotsford–Mission -4.9%, Kitchener–Waterloo -4.4%, London -4.3%. Largest rises: Fredericton +5.1%, Halifax +4.4%, Winnipeg +3.9%, Saskatoon +3.9%. Direction agrees with the change vs 2025-Q1 in 23 of 24 places. CAUTION: StatCan marks 2025-Q2 estimates as modelled (one listing platform was unavailable), so treat the year-on-year figure as indicative. These are advertised-price changes, not changes in what sitting tenants pay.
findings.calc: (asking 1-bedroom apartment rent 2026-Q2 / 2025-Q2 - 1) x 100 from published rounded values; median across 24 places with both values.

findings.headline: Since 2019 advertised 1-bedroom rents are up most in Sherbrooke (+83%) and least in Toronto (+6%)
findings.detail: Latest (2026-Q2) 1-bedroom asking rent vs the mean of the four 2019 quarters: median +43%. Biggest increases: Sherbrooke +83%, Greater Sudbury +82%, Fredericton +74%, Halifax +69%, Moncton +69%; smallest: Toronto +6%, Vancouver +21%, Edmonton +22%, Hamilton +26%. Dollar rents are nominal (not adjusted for general inflation). The 2019 base comes from the first quarters of an experimental listings series, when listing coverage may have been thinner, so very large percentage rises should be read as 'substantially higher', not as exact.

stat.label: median change in 1-bedroom asking rent vs 2019 average

findings.calc: (asking 1-bedroom rent 2026-Q2 / mean(2019-Q1..Q4) - 1) x 100, nominal dollars; places with all four 2019 quarters.

findings.headline: Advertised 2-bedroom rents sit a median 17% above CMHC's average rent; the gap ranges from -1% to +43%
findings.detail: Asking rent for 2-bedroom apartments in 2025-Q4 (StatCan) vs CMHC's October 2025 average rent for purpose-built apartments, 26 places. Largest gaps: Montréal +43% (asking $1,920 vs $1,346), Hamilton +32% (asking $2,190 vs $1,656), Vancouver +31% (asking $3,090 vs $2,363), Toronto +30% (asking $2,670 vs $2,046); smallest: Saskatoon -1%, Calgary +1%, Edmonton +1%. The gap is not 'overpricing': the two measure different things - units advertised for rent during a quarter on listing platforms (new leases, any building type) vs a survey of the average rent across all units in purpose-built rental structures of 3+ units, including long-standing tenancies. For a newcomer, the asking rent is the better guide to what a new lease costs.

stat.label: median asking vs CMHC average rent gap, 2-bedroom

findings.calc: (asking 2-bedroom apartment rent, REF_DATE 2025-10 / CMHC table 1.1.2 average rent 2-bedroom Oct-25 - 1) x 100; Ottawa/Gatineau use provincial parts; places in both sources.

findings.headline: In the 16 cities with a rent CPI, rents already being paid changed by between -4.9% and +9.5% over the 12 months to 2026-09
findings.detail: 12-month change in the CPI 'rented accommodation' index (rent and related tenant costs), Victoria +9.5%, St. John's +8.9%, Charlottetown +8.0%, Thunder Bay +7.9%, Halifax +7.0% at the top and Calgary -4.9%, Edmonton -0.1%, Saskatoon +1.7%, Toronto +1.8% at the bottom. CPI measures change in rents of the existing rental stock (including renewals), so it can differ in direction from asking rents on new listings. It says nothing about which city is cheaper. Charlottetown's value covers Charlottetown and Summerside; other places without a city CPI use provincial values (see map layer flags).
findings.calc: CPI 'Rented accommodation' index (2002=100), 2026-09 / same month a year earlier - 1, x 100, for the cities StatCan publishes in table 18-10-0004-01.

interpretation: For a first apartment, the asking rent is the number to budget with: it reflects units a newcomer can actually apply for today. The lowest asking rents here are in Quebec (Sherbrooke, Québec City), parts of the Prairies (Regina, Edmonton) and some Atlantic cities (Saint John), while Halifax is among the higher-rent places; the ranking is only about price, not wages, job availability or vacancy.

The CMHC average covers all units in purpose-built rental buildings, including long-standing tenancies whose rent only changes at renewal (and, in some provinces, within increase limits), so it describes a different, slower-moving part of the market than new listings; the CPI rent index likewise tracks rents of the existing rental stock.
A fall in asking rents over a year does not mean cheap housing is easy to find: check vacancy rates (CMHC) alongside, and view listings directly.
methodology: Asking rents: StatCan table 46-10-0092-01 (experimental Quarterly Rent Statistics), average asking rent for apartments by bedroom count in each CMA, rounded to $10 by StatCan; Ottawa and Gatineau use the Ontario and Quebec parts of the CMA.
Change since 2019 compares the latest quarter with the mean of the four 2019 quarters; 1-year change compares with the same quarter a year earlier.

CMHC: Rental Market Survey, October 2025, average rent by bedroom type for private apartments in structures of 3+ units, per centre (CMA/CA); the asking-vs-CMHC comparison uses asking rent for 2025-Q4 (the quarter containing the October survey) to match timing.
CPI: 12-month change in 'rented accommodation' (the rent sub-index published at city level), table 18-10-0004-01, latest month.
limitations: Asking rents are advertised prices from online platforms, not signed leases; they exclude subsidised units, lease transfers and short-term rentals, and coverage varies by city and size of rental market.
StatCan flags 2025-Q2 and Q3 estimates as modelled (one platform unavailable); year-on-year changes use 2025-Q2 as the comparison quarter and are indicative.
Experimental series starting 2019: early-2019 estimates may be less well-covered; percentage rises since 2019 are nominal.
CMHC covers purpose-built rental structures of 3+ units only; asking rents cover all listed rental apartments in the CMA. The two are not the same population and the gap is not an error measure.

Not covered by StatCan asking rents: Charlottetown, Brandon, Whitehorse, Yellowknife, Iqaluit (CMHC covers Charlottetown and Yellowknife only). CPI is a price-change measure and is published for only some cities.
